فهم المقروء:
1) When an antibiotic is described as losing its power, the wording suggests that the drug has changed. It has not. What has changed is the population of bacteria it is used against. In any large population a few individuals happen to carry a feature that lets them survive the drug, and when the drug is applied the rest die and those few are left to multiply. The drug has not weakened; it has selected.
2) The features themselves are varied. Some bacteria produce an enzyme that cuts the drug apart before it can act. Others alter the exact part of the cell the drug is built to attack, so that it no longer fits. Others pump the drug back out through the cell wall as fast as it enters. None of these is an invention made in response to treatment; each already existed somewhere in the population, often at a very low frequency, long before the drug was used.
3) What makes bacteria different from larger organisms is how fast such a feature can travel. Bacteria do not only pass their genes to their descendants; they also exchange small rings of genetic material directly with neighbours, including neighbours of a different species. A resistance gene that arises in one kind of bacterium in one patient can therefore appear, within a short time, in an unrelated kind in a different place.
4) Two practices accelerate the process more than any other. The first is stopping a course of treatment early, when the patient feels better: the most susceptible bacteria are dead, the hardier ones are not, and the course has been turned into a filter. The second is the routine use of antibiotics in healthy livestock to speed growth, which exposes enormous bacterial populations to low doses continuously, a condition close to ideal for selection.
5) Finding new drugs is harder than it was. The easy sources have been searched, the cost of taking a candidate through trials is high, and a new antibiotic is held in reserve rather than sold widely, which makes it a poor investment compared with a drug for a chronic condition. Several large companies have left the field altogether.
6) The practical conclusion is unwelcome but clear. Since the supply of new drugs cannot be relied on, the existing ones have to be treated as a stock that can be spent. That means prescribing them only where they can work, finishing the courses that are started, and keeping them out of agriculture — none of which is a discovery, and all of which is a change in behaviour rather than in medicine.

فهم المقروء:
1) In a place where rain is rare and rivers do not run, the water that exists is usually underground, and the problem is not finding it but moving it without losing it. A pump raises water and spends fuel; an open channel carries it and loses much of it to the sun. The solution developed across the dry belt from Iran to Oman and into North Africa does neither. It lets gravity do the moving and keeps the water underground for most of the journey.
2) The method begins with a mother well, dug at the foot of high ground until it reaches water. From the well a tunnel is cut, sloping very gently downwards, running for anything from a few hundred metres to tens of kilometres until it emerges at the surface near the land to be irrigated. The gradient is the whole difficulty: too steep and the flowing water cuts into the floor of the tunnel and collapses it; too shallow and the water stands still and the channel silts up.
3) Along the line of the tunnel a row of vertical shafts is sunk at intervals, and from the air these shafts are the clearest sign of the system, a line of pale rings crossing the desert. They were used to remove the excavated spoil, to admit air for the diggers, and afterwards to give access for repair. A tunnel that is not cleaned will close within a few seasons.
4) What is less often noticed is that the design also distributes. The flow at the outlet is continuous, so the question is not how much water each farmer gets but for how long. Shares are measured in time, traditionally by a sundial or a water clock, and these shares can be inherited, sold or rented. A right to a quarter of an hour at a known interval is a piece of property, and the records of such rights are among the older documents of the region.
5) The weakness is precisely the strength. The system gives a steady flow that depends on the level of the groundwater, and it cannot be increased when demand rises. Where modern pumps have been installed nearby, they lower the water table, the tunnel runs dry, and a structure maintained for centuries stops working within a few years for reasons that have nothing to do with its construction.
6) The engineering is often admired as a relic, which misses the more useful point. The design is an answer to a question still being asked: how to take water out of the ground at a rate that does not exceed what returns to it. The tunnels answered it by physical limit rather than by rule, and that is harder to argue with.

فهم المقروء:
1) The desert locust spends most of its history as an unremarkable insect. Scattered thinly across a band of dry country from West Africa to India, it lives alone, avoids its own kind, and is green or sandy in colour. In this state it is of no interest to anyone but the entomologist, and populations can persist for years without attracting a single report.
2) The change begins with rain. Unusual rainfall in a breeding area produces vegetation, the vegetation allows more eggs to survive, and the survivors are pushed together as the plants dry back and the remaining green patches shrink. Crowding is the trigger. An insect that repeatedly touches others of its kind undergoes a transformation over a generation or two: it turns yellow and black, becomes active instead of retiring, and begins to seek the company it formerly avoided.
3) The crowded form is what the world calls a plague. Bands of wingless young march across the ground; adults form swarms that can cover hundreds of square kilometres and travel with the prevailing wind rather than against it, which is why a swarm leaving the Red Sea coast may arrive in a country that has had no rain at all. A swarm eats roughly its own weight each day, and the weight of a large swarm is measured in thousands of tonnes.
4) Because the transformation needs particular conditions in particular places, it can be anticipated. Satellites show where rain has fallen and where the ground has turned green, and survey teams visit those areas to look for the early signs: eggs in the soil, bands forming, colour beginning to change. The purpose is not to count insects but to find the few places where crowding is about to begin.
5) Control is then a matter of timing. A band of young on the ground can be treated in a small area at low cost; the same insects as a flying swarm must be chased across borders and sprayed from aircraft at many times the expense, often over land that belongs to someone else. Every week of delay multiplies both the area and the price.
6) The difficulty is that the cheap moment is also the invisible one. It occurs in remote country, often where surveys are hardest to run, and it asks governments to spend money on an insect that no farmer has yet complained about. The plagues that reach the news are, almost by definition, the ones where that argument was lost.

In the summer of 1854, cholera swept through a crowded district of London. The accepted explanation was bad air rising from the river, and few doctors questioned it. A physician named John Snow doubted the theory. Instead of arguing, he walked the streets and marked every death on a map of the neighbourhood. The marks clustered tightly around a single water pump on Broad Street. Households that drew their water elsewhere were largely spared, and a nearby workhouse with its own well lost almost no one. Snow took his map to the local officials and asked them to remove the pump handle. They were unconvinced by his reasoning but agreed to the measure, and the outbreak faded soon afterwards. It took years before the medical establishment accepted that water, not air, had carried the disease. The map had done what the argument alone could not: it made the pattern impossible to ignore.

One effective solution is to improve public transportation. For example, the city could increase the number of buses and make them more reliable and comfortable. Alfred Wegener was a meteorologist, not a geologist, and that may be why he asked the question. Looking at a world map, he noticed that the coast of South America seemed to fit the coast of Africa, as though the two had once been joined. Others had noticed the resemblance and dismissed it as coincidence. Wegener gathered evidence instead: identical fossils of land animals on both shores, matching rock formations, and signs of ancient ice in places that are now tropical. In 1912 he proposed that the continents had drifted apart. Geologists rejected the idea almost unanimously, and their objection was reasonable: he could not explain what force could move a continent. He died on an expedition to Greenland with the argument unresolved. Half a century later, surveys of the ocean floor revealed spreading ridges, and the mechanism he had lacked was found. The evidence had been right; the explanation had not yet been invented.

فهم المقروء:
A queue that moves steadily feels shorter than a queue of the same length that stops and starts, even when the wait is identical. Research on waiting has produced a set of findings that are consistent enough to design around. Unoccupied time feels longer than occupied time, which is why mirrors near lifts and information screens in stations reduce complaints without reducing the wait. Uncertain waits feel longer than known ones: a sign saying the next train arrives in nine minutes is more tolerable than no sign at all, even when nine minutes is the longer wait. Unexplained waits feel longest of all, and an announcement giving a reason reliably lowers irritation. And people tolerate a long wait for something they value far better than a short wait for something they do not. None of this shortens anything. It is a reminder that the experience being managed is not the duration but the perception of it — and that the two can be improved separately.
